newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian pension reform biggest problem -finmin.
newsitem.headline: Croatian pension reform biggest problem -finmin.

text.p: Croatian Finance Minister Bozo Prka said on Thursday a reform of the country's ailing pension system, seen as its main long-term fiscal problem, would cost annually three percent of GDP for 10 years from launch.

"Croatia's biggest long-term problem are pensioners, there is a constant pressure for solving it. It is probably the most acute and the most complicated problem of the fiscal policy," Prka told Reuters in an interview.

Prka said he saw the transition from the current "pay-as-you-go" system to a combined saving system within two years: "A reform of the pension system is urgent. I see it implemented within two years."
He put the annual cost of the reform at some three percent of the country's gross domestic product (GDP) for at least 10 years from launch.

"That would be a transitional cost that has to be financed from the budget. Present transfers to the pension fund would have to be increased as a lot of young people would come out of the present system and make contributions to the new one," Prka said.
The finance ministry put the 1997 GDP at 108 billion kuna ($17.8 billion).

Since the bulk of the money for the reform will have to come from the budget, it will put pressure on the country's ambitious plan to stay within the Maastricht criteria for debt and deficit. The 1997 budget deficit was projected at 2.63 percent of GDP.
But Prka said the state would make use of the parallel process of privatisation of the large public sector, including utilities and other large state-owned companies like the oil monopoly INA.
"The revenues from privatising the public sector could be partly used for financing the transition costs of the pension reform," Prka said.

The new pension system would be a so called "three-pillar" system, based on three elements: obligatory contributions to the public pension fund, also obligatory contributions but to the investment funds, and voluntary, private arrangements.
Prka said a legal framework for the reform was already in the works.

The government proposed to raise the age-limit for retirement, and a new formula for calculating pensions which will adjust them with the inflation as opposed the salaries, clearing them of quasi-social elements.
Croatia has increasingly ageing population of 4.7 million, and some 1.5 million employed have to support around 890,000 pensioners. -- Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075 ($ = 6.071 Croatian Kuna)
